chunks: Ali ibn Muhammad, from Sahl ibn Ziyad, from Ali ibn al-Rayyan, who said:

I wrote to him: 'A man is in a house, and its walls prevent him from looking at the redness of the sunset (Al-Maghrib) and recognizing the disappearance of the twilight, and the time for the last prayer of Al-Isha. When should he pray it, and how should he deal with it?' So he (peace be upon him) signed: 'He should pray it when it is upon this description, at the abundance of the stars; and Al-Maghrib is at their clashing, and the whiteness of the disappearance of the sun [is] the abundance of the stars until their clarity.'
ai.seo_question: How to determine prayer times when you cannot see the sky from inside a house?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Al-Kafi* establishes the principle of *istishab* (presumption of continuity) and practical estimation (*takhmin*) for prayer times when direct observation of celestial signs is obstructed. It highlights the Shia scholarly reliance on the 'clashing' (*ishtibak*) of stars for Maghrib and their distinct clarity (*bayān*) for the last Isha, providing a precise astronomical benchmark for those indoors. This ruling underscores the flexibility in Islamic jurisprudence to accommodate environmental constraints while maintaining strict adherence to the defined prayer windows.
